1:
The turn from Egypt to Philistia is read as a turn from false friends to open enemies. Gill notes that the former prophecies were against the Egyptians, the friends and allies of the Jews in whom they trusted, and that this one is against their near neighbours and implacable enemies. Henry puts the contrast more sharply: as the Egyptians had often proved false friends, so the Philistines had always been sworn enemies to the Israel of God, the more dangerous for being such near neighbours; they were humbled in the time of David but had got head again and were a considerable people until Nebuchadnezzar cut them off. Calvin asks what the prophecy was for, and answers from the other side of the border. The Philistines had contrived many cruel and unjust things against the Israelites, and God intended by this word to testify his love towards them, undertaking their cause and avenging their wrongs; and so he gave them a reason for patience, since they had to wait until he fulfilled it.

The date is where the commentators divide. Clarke says plainly that it cannot easily be ascertained, and reports two proposals, one placing it about the fourth year of Zedekiah and the other somewhere in the reign of Josiah. Ellicott fixes it more narrowly. The message belongs with an earlier list of nations, the Gaza of this verse being the Azzah of that, and its date falls before the attack of Necho on the city; writers who identify a city named in an ancient history with Gaza put that attack on his return from Carchemish, so the prophecy falls between the two events. Henry, without fixing the year, canvasses three occasions for the blow itself: whether the king of Egypt gave it in his expedition against Carchemish, or on his return after he had slain Josiah, or when he afterwards came to relieve Jerusalem.

Why the note of time is added at all is answered the same way by Henry and Wesley. It is mentioned, Henry says, to show that this word came when the Philistines were in their full strength and lustre, their cities in good condition and in no peril from any adversary; when no disturbance of their repose was foreseen by any human probabilities, their ruin was foretold, and the smiting of Gaza soon after would be only an earnest of it and the beginning of sorrows. Wesley says it in six words: in the time of Philistine prosperity. On the smiting itself Clarke and Ellicott are directly at odds. Clarke states that we have no historical relation of any Egyptian king smiting Gaza, that it was no doubt smitten by one of them but that when and by whom does not appear either from sacred or profane history; Ellicott treats the attack as identifiable and uses it to date the prophecy.

What befell the Philistines in the end is placed differently again. Clarke supposes the calamities predicted here fell upon them during the long siege of Tyre, when their country was desolated to prevent their giving Tyre or Sidon any assistance, while Henry has Nebuchadnezzar simply cut them off. Calvin turns aside to the city and its name. The ancient Gaza, so far as can be found out, stood near the sea, and after it was destroyed another was built, the one mentioned by Luke, which heathen writers describe as celebrated and opulent. Those are mistaken, he says, who derive the name from a Persic word meaning treasures on the ground that Cambyses left his riches there; the word is a very ancient Hebrew one, and Gaza takes its name not from treasures but from a term signifying fortitude or strength. Clarke pauses on the writing rather than the history, calling the whole chapter remarkably elegant and the address to the sword of the Lord at its close a particularly beautiful and bold personification.
2:
The rising waters are read as an army by all. Gill takes them for a host of men coming in great numbers and with great rapidity, like an overflowing flood, and reports the Targum to the same effect. Clarke calls waters a common prophetic image for a multitude of people, and says the north here means Chaldea. Ellicott makes the same identification an argument: the reference to the north indicates that the invasion contemplated is that of Nebuchadnezzar and not of Pharaoh-necho; and he corrects the following clause, where for the land and all that is therein one should read, with the margin, the land and the fulness thereof.

Calvin builds a reading on the distinction between the two invaders. The prophet wished to remind the Jews that the plundering of Gaza would be only a prelude, a far more grievous punishment impending over that ungodly nation. Had Gaza suffered only that loss, the Jews might have complained of their own lot, seeing men who had so provoked God’s vengeance lightly punished, and might have said: God has indeed smitten Gaza lightly, but we would willingly redeem our lives at that price, as men who wish to avoid shipwreck cast their goods into the sea, parting with all their property if only life be given them. Hence the prophet says that something more grievous awaited the city. When you see Gaza plundered, Calvin has him say, that is not the last judgment of God: the Egyptians shall only plunder the city’s wealth, which will be endurable, but at length the Chaldeans will come with boundless cruelty, and be like a flood, and overwhelm it utterly. There is implied a comparison between the Egyptian plunder and the final Chaldean ruin.

Keil and Delitzsch report the argument over that heading. Two of the commentators they cite place the capture of Gaza in the march of Necho against the Assyrians, one before the battle at Megiddo and the other after it, on the assumption, shared by all modern expositors, that Necho had landed at the Bay of Acre. The second supports this by observing that Necho, before marching farther north, sought to keep his way of retreat clear, since he would otherwise have been lost after Carchemish had he not previously reduced Gaza, the key of the high road to Egypt. And in this, Keil and Delitzsch say, he rightly assumes that the heading was not meant to show the prophecy fulfilled in the conquest of Gaza by Necho, but merely states that the prophet predicts destruction by a foe from the north at a time when such conquest was impending.

Why the fathers do not turn back is explained two ways. Ellicott makes it a moral failure: the selfishness of panic reaches its highest point and crushes out the instincts of natural affection, so that even fathers are content to save themselves regardless of their children. Clarke and Calvin make it incapacity instead. Clarke says that though their children are left behind they have neither strength nor courage to bring them off; Calvin argues that men even in adversity do not divest themselves of their natural feelings, and that a father would willingly undergo ten deaths to save his children, so that forgetting they are parents proves the greatest grief, as though they had become logs of wood. By dissolution of hands, he adds, is meant loss of courage, for as vigour spreads from the heart through the body, the hands being the chief instruments of all action, and when they are relaxed men become as it were inanimate, not moving so much as a finger, having lost their senses at the stamping of horses and the rumbling of wheels. Gill hears the noise as the cavalry of Nebuchadnezzar heard at a distance; Clarke praises the rendering, in which the translators sought to convey the sense by the sound of the words.
4:
Gill says the day named is the time the Lord appointed for a destruction that should be universal. Why Tyre and Zidon are named alongside Philistia is answered three ways. Clarke says the two cities belonged to the Phoenicians and were depending on the succour of their allies the Philistines, whose expectation was cut off; Wesley reverses the direction, saying Tyre and Sidon were neighbours to the Philistines and were often called to their aid. Ellicott finds the traffic running the other way again: in the helper that remaineth he sees a reference to the foreign mercenaries, especially Philistines, employed by the two great commercial cities, and notes that the nations were not infrequently in alliance. Calvin explains the grouping geographically, these being cities of Palestine to which the Philistines were contiguous, so that the prophet rightly includes them in the same bundle; and the destruction was denounced on them especially so that the Jews might know nothing would be safe in the whole land when these cities, the defences of the whole country, were destined to perish.

Caphtor is harder. Clarke offers Crete or Cyprus, or a coastal district belonging to the Philistines, or the Cappadocians. Ellicott lists five identifications, Crete, Cyprus, Caria, Cappadocia and the delta of the Nile, and inclines to the last, since the ethnological table connects both peoples with Egypt and a passage in Amos points to a migration of the Philistines from that region, so that there is a touch of scorn in calling them the mere remnant of Caphtor. Wesley takes the Egyptian view without argument, the two peoples being related because their first progenitors were sons of Mizriam.

The baldness on Gaza is agreed to be mourning. Clarke says they have cut off their hair in token of deep sorrow, and takes the next clause as Ashkelon put to silence, another mark of the deepest sorrow; Ellicott calls it the outward sign of extremest mourning and perhaps of extremest desolation, and prefers to render the other clause as Ashkelon is speechless. Calvin says the prophet returns to what is figurative in order to move the Jews more powerfully, and reports the custom behind it, that they were wont even to tear their faces with their nails and pluck off their hair; by the tearing he understands mourning, and takes the point to be that there would be no end to their calamities.

The remnant of their valley parts the readings furthest. Clarke takes the valley as the plain, since the whole land of the Philistines was a vast plain extending along the coast from Phoenicia to Egypt, and says the whole of it shall be desolated; Wesley takes it of those who lived in the valleys near Ashkelon. Ellicott canvasses three possibilities: the Greek version apparently followed a different text and gives the remnant of the Anakim, which one critic adopts and connects with the fact that a remnant of the old gigantic race had taken refuge among the Philistines after being driven from Hebron; others take the word rendered their valley to mean those who speak an unintelligible tongue, barbarians, supposing the form to have passed into the more familiar Anakim; but the English version is accepted by many critics and may refer to Ashkelon and Gaza as the last resource of the low country. Calvin reads the word as depth and turns it into a rebuke of confidence: the people dwelt in deep and hidden places and thought themselves secure, like men hid in caverns hard of access, and the prophet derides that confidence, since no place is so deep that the vengeance of God will not penetrate it. On the cutting of themselves Ellicott sees a ritual of supplication prevailing among the Philistines, like that of the priests of Baal, while Wesley turns the question into a rebuke: why afflict themselves when all their mourning will do no good?.
6:
Whose sword it is nobody doubts. Gill says that though it was the sword of the Chaldeans, being appointed and sent by the Lord and directed by his providence to do his will, it is called his sword. Calvin admires the device: the prophet turns to address the sword of God, a happy apostrophe, striking and forcible when he addresses now the land of the Philistines and now the sword itself, with no object but to confirm a prophecy the Jews might otherwise have doubted; the intimation is that the slaughter would be as it were by God’s sword, or by a sword hired by him, the Chaldeans doing his work. Clarke calls the passage a most grand personification, a dialogue between the sword of the Lord and the prophet, than which nothing can be imagined more sublime.

Who speaks the entreaty parts the four. Clarke takes it as the prophet’s own plea: shed no more blood, destroy no more lives, erase no more cities, desolate no more countries; hast thou not been long enough at this work of judgment? let wars and desolations cease for ever. Ellicott gives the words to the victims, as the question and entreaty of the Philistines asking when there will be an end of war. Calvin takes a middle course, making the prophet speak in another’s person: he assumes a character, as though he wished to soothe the sword of God with blandishments and mitigate its fury, saying, O sword, spare them, leave off to rage against the Philistines. The prophet had no such feeling, Calvin says, but it was common with the prophets to assume different characters while confirming their doctrine, and they often speak in the person of those on whom they denounce the vengeance of God. It is as though the Philistines would humbly ask pardon of the sword, but without profit; and then the prophet as it were reproves himself, that he acts foolishly in wishing to repress the sword of God, since it cannot rest.

The answer is put in the sword’s own mouth by Clarke: I am the officer of God’s judgments, and he has given me a commission against Ashkelon and the sea shore, all the coast where the Philistines have their territories, the measure of their iniquities being full. Clarke adds his own reasons: the Philistines were ever the implacable enemies of the Jews and the basest of all idolaters, and on these accounts the sword did its office most fearfully and effectually by the hand of the Chaldeans. Wesley makes the answer God’s rather than the sword’s, God letting the prophet know that he had given the sword its commission, so that it could not stop till Ashkelon and the people on the sea shore were destroyed. Gill states it flatly: there is no reason to believe the sword will be quiet; to stop it is impossible, and to request that it be stopped is in vain.

What the sea shore covers is a smaller question. Calvin reports that some understand Joppa by it, but thinks it probable that the prophet includes the whole coast and is still speaking of Tyre and Sidon and Gaza, though he names Ashkelon, which lay a little distant from the sea; where God commanded his sword against Ashkelon and all the cities by the sea shore, the execution of his judgment could not be prevented. Calvin makes most of the last word of the chapter, which he renders as a solemn protest: God had not simply commanded his sword to commit slaughter through the whole land, but bound it as by a protest, as though the decree could not be revoked, since he will not only command his sword to execute his vengeance but bind it by an oath never to cease until the whole people, and all the cities, and the whole land, are destroyed together.
